resident.chief_complaint: Progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, now unable to walk without a walking aid.
resident.history: Fifty-one-year-old delivery man with no significant past medical history presented with progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, worsening to inability to walk without a walking aid. He also had chronic neck stiffness for over two years and had not sought intervention. He denied any difficulty with hand dexterity, such as using chopsticks, buttoning a shirt, or picking up a coin.
resident.physical_exam: Neurological examination revealed signs of myelopathy in the lower limbs. MRC muscle power grading in both lower limbs (L2-S1) was 4/5. Deep tendon reflexes, including knee jerk and ankle jerk, were exaggerated bilaterally. Babinski's sign was positive bilaterally. The patient had difficulty getting up from an armless chair and was unable to perform tandem gait. No upper limb signs were demonstrated: sensory-motor function and reflexes were normal in both upper limbs, and Hoffman's sign was negative.
key_positive_signs: Exaggerated knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes bilaterally
Difficulty rising from an armless chair
resident.past_history: No significant past medical history. Chronic neck stiffness for over two years, for which he did not seek intervention.
resident.public_message: A 51-year-old man presented with six months of progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness, now requiring a walking aid, and chronic neck stiffness for over two years. Examination showed bilateral lower limb weakness (MRC 4/5), exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, difficulty rising from a chair, and inability to tandem gait; upper limbs were neurologically normal. JOA score was 14/17 (grade 1 disability). Cervical spine X-rays showed degeneration with loss of lordosis and anterior osteophytes C3-C6; CT and MRI showed extensive OPLL from C3 to T3 causing significant canal compromise with no cord signal changes. Diagnosis: extensive cervicothoracic OPLL causing myelopathy.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; the films were not available for review. CT and MRI were described as showing extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) from C3-T3 with significant canal compromise. No cord signal change was reported. The direction of compression and a graded severity of stenosis were not stated. The described imaging has high correlation with the reported myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy. Bilateral lower limb weakness with exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, and positive Babinski signs indicate corticospinal tract dysfunction. The absence of upper limb motor, sensory, or reflex abnormalities and a negative Hoffman sign, together with no documented sensory level or sphincter disturbance, means the clinical level cannot be pinpointed to the cervical cord alone; it is compatible with lower cervical or upper thoracic cord involvement. The OPLL from C3 to T3 provides a structural correlate. Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is well recognized in OPLL because the laterally placed lower-limb fibers in the corticospinal tract and the longest axons are most vulnerable to anterior compression. The examination is incomplete as lower limb sensory function, sensory level, and sphincter function are not documented.

red_flags.finding: Normal upper limb motor/sensory/reflexes and negative Hoffman despite OPLL from C3.
red_flags.rationale: Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is common in OPLL because the lower-limb corticospinal fibers are more laterally placed and more vulnerable to anterior compression, and early disease often spares the upper limbs. This does not offer an alternative cause and does not change the levels already identified by imaging.

red_flags.finding: No cord T2 signal change on MRI.
red_flags.rationale: Absence of T2 hyperintensity does not exclude clinically significant myelopathy, especially in early or dynamic compression. It is not an alternative explanation and does not alter the indication; it may suggest less severe cord damage but does not change the plan.

red_flags.finding: Incomplete documentation of lower limb sensory exam, sensory level, and sphincter function.
red_flags.rationale: The missing data limit precise clinical localization and cannot confirm a sensory level matching the imaged OPLL. However, the upper motor neuron signs already establish a myelopathy above the lumbosacral enlargement, so this gap does not change the diagnosis or the surgical plan.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: There is no fundamental mismatch: the imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise that can explain the bilateral lower limb upper motor neuron syndrome. Notable but non-contradictory observations are the absence of upper limb signs despite C3 involvement and absent cord signal change; both are consistent with early, leg-predominant cervical/thoracic myelopathy. The exact symptomatic level cannot be determined from the examination because lower limb sensory level and sphincter function were not documented.
neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy; the absence of upper limb signs means the clinical level is likely lower cervical or upper thoracic, not definitively C3. The imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise, which explains the dominant lower-limb syndrome; the symptom-imaging match is high. Notable findings are all coexisting and do not change the indication or plan: (1) normal upper limbs despite C3 involvement—common in early leg-predominant OPLL; (2) no cord T2 signal—does not exclude myelopathy; (3) incomplete sensory/sphincter documentation—limits precise level but not diagnosis. There is no evidence of coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative MAP target 75 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk moderate. Prone position tolerance moderate. Extubation difficulty unassessable: no airway assessment on record.

preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of lower limb weakness or gait instability, such as new falls or inability to walk even with an aid
Development of new upper limb symptoms, sphincter dysfunction, or a drop in JOA score by 2 or more points
No stabilization or improvement of neurological status after 3 months of structured conservative treatment
Evidence of new or progressive cord signal change on follow-up MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge that progressive myelopathy carries a risk with delay. However, the absence of cord signal change on MRI and the relatively preserved JOA score (14/17) leave a narrow window for a time-limited, closely monitored conservative trial. A structured program of physical therapy, gait training, activity modification, and serial neurological assessments could be offered for 3-6 months, provided the patient is fully informed and there is immediate access to surgical evaluation if any failure criterion is met. This approach is not without risk, but surgery for extensive OPLL also carries significant morbidity, and early intervention may still be possible if deterioration occurs.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director has pointed to the documented clinical progression over six months as the key indication for surgery, arguing that this outweighs the absence of cord signal change. I have already weighed that progression in my initial assessment: it is gradual, the patient remains ambulatory with a walking aid, JOA is 14/17 with no upper limb or sphincter involvement, and there is no cord signal change on MRI. That absence of signal change remains a meaningful indicator that the cord is not yet irreversibly damaged, supporting a narrow, closely monitored window for conservative treatment. The progression itself does not negate the possibility of a successful conservative trial when failure criteria are clearly defined and immediate surgical referral is available. No new finding from the record has been cited that I have given too little weight, so I maintain my recommendation for a time-limited conservative approach.

vice_opinions.assessment: A 51-year-old man with progressive myelopathy due to extensive C3-T3 OPLL causing significant canal compromise. Despite no cord T2 signal change and JOA 14/17, the documented six-month deterioration with lower limb weakness and gait impairment indicates ongoing neurological decline. Without surgical decompression, there is a high risk of irreversible spinal cord injury. Surgical intervention is indicated, but the optimal approach and extent require further imaging clarification and multidisciplinary input.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression and stabilization: C3-C7 laminoplasty (or laminectomy with instrumented fusion) extended to T3 as needed, addressing the compressive OPLL from C3 to T3.
Anterior decompression (corpectomy or direct OPLL resection) at the most compressive levels, possibly combined with posterior fusion.
Time-limited supervised conservative management with serial neurological monitoring as proposed by the physiatrist, with surgery if deterioration occurs.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression and stabilization: C3-C7 laminoplasty (or laminectomy with instrumented fusion) extended to T3 as needed, addressing the compressive OPLL from C3 to T3.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist’s proposal for a conservative trial conflicts with the generally accepted indication for surgery in progressive myelopathy; delay risks irreversible cord damage.

The absence of cord T2 signal change and mild JOA do not eliminate the need for early surgical intervention; these may indicate earlier-stage myelopathy but not a reason to defer in the face of documented progression.

The exact direction of compression and presence of kyphotic deformity were not clearly defined on imaging; this influences whether posterior decompression alone is sufficient or whether anterior or combined approaches are needed.
deferred_questions_to_director: Can we obtain or re-review the actual imaging to clarify the direction of compression (anterior vs posterior) and the degree of canal stenosis, to guide choice of approach?
What is the director’s view on the physiatrist’s conservative trial as an alternative? Should it be offered to the patient if he prefers to avoid surgery initially?
Should the decompression include the thoracic segments T1-T3, given the OPLL extends to T3, or is cervical decompression sufficient?
If posterior surgery is chosen, do you favor laminoplasty versus laminectomy with fusion, given the loss of lordosis?
vice_opinions.public_message: This patient has progressive myelopathy from extensive C3-T3 OPLL. Despite no cord signal change and a relatively preserved JOA, the clear clinical progression over six months makes surgical decompression my preferred option to prevent further deterioration. I favor posterior decompression/stabilization, but the exact approach and extent must be tailored after reviewing the imaging. I acknowledge the physiatrist’s conservative trial, but I worry that delay may allow irreversible cord injury. I welcome the group’s input and the director’s guidance on these open questions.

vice_opinions.assessment: This patient has progressive cervical/upper thoracic myelopathy due to extensive OPLL. The clear progression over six months with new walking aid requirement and myelopathic signs outweighs the absence of T2 cord signal change. Surgical decompression is indicated to halt progression and maximize recovery; delaying for a conservative trial risks irreversible cord injury. I favour a posterior decompression with instrumented fusion as the initial approach, given the long-segment pathology and likely need to address multilevel compression, but the final construct depends on imaging details (direction of compression, kyphosis, stability).
proposed_options: Posterior decompression (laminectomy or laminoplasty) with instrumented fusion from C3 to T3, possibly extended to C2 or T4 depending on OPLL extent and instability.
Combined anterior-posterior decompression if imaging shows dominant anterior compression or significant kyphosis that cannot be addressed posteriorly.
Anterior decompression alone (e.g., multilevel corpectomy) if the pathology is focal anterior and the spine is stable without kyphosis.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression with instrumented fusion (laminectomy and lateral mass/pedicle screw fixation) from C3 to T3, with exact upper/lower instrumented levels determined after review of imaging and flexion-extension views.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's claim that the absence of cord signal change indicates less severe cord damage and supports a safe conservative trial is not evidence-based in OPLL; clinical progression is the paramount risk factor for irreversible injury, and this patient has clear progression over six months.

A time-limited conservative trial, even with monitoring, would expose the patient to a risk of stepwise deterioration that may not be reversible; I would not offer it as an equal alternative now that progressive myelopathy is documented.

We need to clarify whether the normal upper limbs suggest a lower cervical/upper thoracic level of maximum compression; this may allow a shorter construct if the compression is truly below C5, but the OPLL extends to T3, so a long segment is likely needed.
deferred_questions_to_director: Would you agree that surgical decompression should proceed without a conservative trial, given the clear progression and the risk of irreversible cord injury?
Given the extensive OPLL, do you intend the posterior construct to extend from C2 to T4, or would you consider stopping at C3-T3 if the flexion-extension views show no instability?
When the actual imaging is reviewed, should we obtain a CT myelogram or dynamic MRI if the direction of compression remains unclear, before finalizing the surgical plan?
vice_opinions.public_message: I agree with the director that surgery is indicated. I favour posterior decompression with instrumented fusion from C3 to T3, with possible extension depending on imaging. I disagree with the physiatrist's contention that the lack of cord signal change allows a safe conservative trial; the documented progression is the key indication. I would appreciate guidance on the definitive extent of fixation and whether additional imaging is needed before proceeding.

director_rulings.reason_for_delay: We are not ruling yet because I require specific views from the Chief Resident and Rehabilitation Physician and clarification from the Radiologist, as per our collective decision-making practice. The discussion continues, and no treatment is being delayed beyond this meeting.

director_rulings.public_message: Thank you all. I agree that surgery is indicated for this progressive myelopathy, but before ruling I will follow our collective practice and ask specifically: (1) Chief Resident, please give your own recommendation on surgical versus conservative management and your preferred approach. (2) Rehabilitation Physician, please state whether you would still offer a time-limited conservative trial given the documented progression, and exactly how you would monitor for failure. I am also ordering cervical flexion-extension X-rays to assess stability. We will reconvene after these views and the imaging review; my position is that surgery is indicated as things stand, and if we operate, posterior decompression with stabilization is likely, but the exact approach depends on imaging. If the imaging shows anterior compression dominant or severe kyphosis, we would adjust the plan. I am not closing the meeting yet; these specific inputs are required before I rule.

director_rulings.final_decision: Proceed with surgical decompression and stabilization for progressive myelopathy due to extensive C3-T3 OPLL. The conservative trial proposed by the physiatrist is declined: the documented progression over six months indicates a high risk of irreversible cord injury, and the absence of cord signal change does not negate that risk. We will obtain cervical flexion-extension X-rays and a formal radiology review of the existing imaging before finalizing the construct, with contingencies for kyphosis or anterior compression.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Posterior decompression (laminectomy) and instrumented fusion from C3 to T3, with exact upper and lower instrumented levels to be confirmed after review of flexion-extension X-rays and detailed imaging. If imaging reveals dominant anterior compression or severe kyphosis, the approach will be adjusted accordingly, potentially including anterior decompression or extension of the construct.
